items.text: We introduce AuK, an open-source foundational model that unifies speech generation and editing through a common interface of natural-language instructions and audio context. To support this broad capability set, we construct approximately 3.03 billion instruction--audio instances and 1.95 million hours of effective supervision across five task families: speech generation, content editing, enhancement and separation, paralinguistic editing, and acoustic editing. items.text: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) but incurs substantial computation and context costs. items.title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
items.text: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that plan over long horizons and act through external tools. Most agents select actions through unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, leaving implicit the procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. items.text: Instruction-guided 3D editing is essential for interactive content creation, yet it faces a significant bottleneck: the severe scarcity of high-quality paired training data. items.title: SAFIRE: Safety-Critical Benchmark for Fine-grained Fire and Smoke Understanding in Multimodal LLMs
items.text: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong progress on vision-language tasks, yet their reliability in safety-critical settings remains underexplored. Fire-smoke understanding is central to public safety and disaster response, but most existing benchmarks lack diverse real-world scenarios and context-aware evaluation. We introduce SAFIRE, a large-scale benchmark for fire-smoke understanding in MLLMs, comprising 83K captioned images from 20 scenarios and 193K multiple-choice VQA (MCVQA) generated from a 9.7K-image subset, spanning 10 evaluation dimensions from basic perception to higher-order reasoning. A GPT-5.4-assisted multi-stage verification pipeline with MLLM majority voting ensures annotation quality. Evaluating ten open-source MLLMs (8B-38B) yields an average accuracy of 61.9%, exposing major gaps in safety-critical reasoning. We further show that adapting vision encoders with only 7% of our domain-specific data boosts fire-scene classification accuracy from 20.1% to 64.5%, indicating that carefully curated data can yield substantial gains even when data volume is limited. All datasets, models, and code are available at https://risys-lab.github.io/SAFIRE/.

items.text: Compressing large-scale neural networks is essential for deploying models on resource-constrained devices. Most existing methods adopt weight pruning or low-bit quantization individually, often resulting in suboptimal compression rates to preserve acceptable performance drops. We introduce a unified framework for simultaneous pruning and low-bit quantization via Bayesian variational learning (\method), which achieves higher compression rates than prior baselines while maintaining comparable performance. The key idea is to employ a spike-and-slab prior to induce sparsity and model quantized weights using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) to enable low-bit precision. Due to the intractability of the objective involving spike-and-slab priors with GMMs, we derive an efficient approximation that facilitates effective compression with minimal accuracy loss. In theory, we provide a consistent result for our proposed variational approach to a sparse and quantized deep neural network. items.title: SentryLine: Evidence-Grounded Question Answering over Evolving Documents in Oncology Care
items.text: Oncology care operates at constant pressure of absorbing rapidly evolving evidence base in biomedicine. The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) addresses this through living guidelines, but the format introduces a new burden: any recommendation can change at any point, across multiple versioned documents. We present SENTRYLINE, a living guideline-aware clinical question answering system. SENTRYLINE retrieves guideline passages through a vectorless hierarchical RAG pipeline and returns a role-specific answer with inline citations, factual and temporal verification reports, and drift detection notes that surface when a guideline has been updated. We construct ASCOBENCH, a benchmark of 405 three-turn conversations across four question categories with gold answers from expert annotators(clinicians), and use test set to evaluate SENTRYLINE against five baselines under an LLM-as-judge framework. Experiments across three generation backbones show consistent improvements over four retrieval baselines and ASCO's guideline assistant, with particularly strong gains on Reasoning and Role-Specific questions where multi-hop synthesis and register adaptation are required

items.text: Full-duplex spoken language models can listen and speak simultaneously, enabling them to handle interruptions and backchannels in human conversation. items.title: RelightFormer: Feed-forward Generative Transformer for Multiview Object Relighting
items.text: Image relighting is traditionally tackled via complex inverse rendering pipelines, which suffer from ill-posed optimization, or single-image generative models that ignore crucial multi-view cues necessary for understanding 3D geometry and material interactions. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art visual quality, photorealistic relighting quality, and strong zero-shot generalization across single-view, multi-view, and novel-view relighting tasks.

items.title: @termix_ai just put agent.family on Robinhood Chain, alongside BNB Chain and Base. Worth actually unpacking why that specific chain matters…
items.text:
@termix_ai just put agent.family on Robinhood Chain, alongside BNB Chain and Base. Worth actually unpacking why that specific chain matters, because the marketing line (right where tokenized stocks are heating up) undersells it.



Robinhood Chain isn't a random L2. It's an Ethereum layer 2 Robinhood built itself on the Arbitrum Orbit stack, mainnet went live July 1 this year, 100ms blocks, settles back to Ethereum for security, and it's purpose built for tokenized real world assets, meaning actual equities and ETFs, not synthetic DeFi wrappers. Gas is paid in plain ETH, no native chain token, which is a deliberate choice to keep the chain feeling like financial infrastructure rather than another speculative L2. Chainlink is the oracle layer, and Robinhood's own Stock Tokens (200+ US equities and ETFs) are live on it across 120+ countries.



Now overlay that with what AACP's Vault Extension actually does, which I went deep on a couple posts back. The Vault Extension exists so an AI agent can operate a client's capital directly, DeFi yield strategies, liquidity positions, on chain purchases, without ever being able to walk off with it. The mechanism is a StrategyVault holding the funds plus a TransactionGuard that only lets the agent call whitelisted protocols, with a hardcoded stop loss checked after every single transaction. Settlement is performance based: the agent earns a cut of returns above target, gets slashed proportionally if it loses money.



Put those two things next to each other and the Robinhood Chain deployment stops looking like a routine multi chain expansion and starts looking like a specific bet: an agent managed portfolio of tokenized equities, running under the same restricted execution model AACP already built for yield farming, on the one chain where the underlying assets are actual regulated stock tokens instead of wrapped synthetic exposure. The Vault Extension's total value calculation already leans on Chainlink price feeds for its stop loss checks, and Chainlink is Robinhood Chain's oracle provider too, so the pricing infrastructure an agent would need to manage a tokenized-stock vault responsibly is arguably already sitting there rather than something TermiX has to bolt on.



One honest gap worth naming: the AACP whitepaper (v0.1, March 2026) lists Base, BNB Chain, and Ethereum as target deployment chains in its Section 11 roadmap. Robinhood Chain isn't in that document at all, so this expansion happened after the spec was written, which either means there's an updated version I haven't seen, or the team is shipping ahead of their own published roadmap. Not a red flag by itself, but it's the kind of thing worth checking the current docs for before treating the whitepaper as the live source of truth on deployment targets.



The bigger read: most "agent economy" chatter still lives entirely on DeFi native rails, agents trading tokens, providing liquidity, arbing pools. Putting AI agent commerce on the same settlement layer as tokenized US equities is a different claim, that agents doing real economic work and regulated financial instruments can share infrastructure without one being a toy version of the other. Whether the Vault Extension is actually being used for anything on Robinhood Chain yet, versus this just being rail laying for later, isn't something I can verify from the outside.



Still just reading and cross referencing announcements against the whitepaper here, haven't registered an identity or touched the product myself.



whitepaper: github.com/TermiX-official/a… (section 10, section 11.1)




Rusan In Crypto (@RusanX)



Been reading the part of the AACP whitepaper most people probably skip: the Vault Extension. It's a separate module from the core "pay an agent for a task" flow, and it's solving a very different problem.



The base protocol handles payment for work: a Client pays, a Provider delivers, everyone settles. But there's a second category of agent commerce that doesn't fit that shape at all, jobs where the Client isn't paying for labor, they're handing the agent actual capital to operate with. Think an agent running a DeFi yield strategy with your funds, or executing onchain purchases on your behalf. The agent has to be able to use the money, but never be able to walk off with it.



Their answer is a StrategyVault plus what they call a TransactionGuard. The Vault holds the client's capital. The Provider gets execution rights inside it, meaning it can call whitelisted protocols like Aave, Uniswap, Compound, but every single call gets checked against a guard contract first. The guard has hardcoded restrictions that can't be configured away: no transferring funds out to non whitelisted addresses, no approvals to random contracts, no delegatecalls. So the agent can move capital around between the vault and approved protocols, but there's no path for it to just leave the perimeter.



There's also a live stop loss. After every transaction, the vault checks total portfolio value against a floor the client set upfront. If a transaction would push value below that floor, it reverts. And separately, a keeper process checks the vault periodically in case external market moves (not the agent's own actions) drag the value down, if that happens, the agent's execution rights get automatically revoked and the vault goes into wind  down mode.



Settlement is tied to actual performance, not just "did the agent do something." If the agent hits the target return, it earns a cut of the excess as a performance fee. If it undershoots but doesn't lose money, it just gets a smaller management fee. If it loses money, its stake gets slashed proportionally to how bad the loss was, and the client gets compensated from that.



What stands out to me is that this is a genuinely different trust problem than the core protocol solves. "Did you do the work" and "did you handle my money responsibly" aren't the same question, and it's easy to see why most agent marketplaces just don't touch the second one.

items.title: It Is Not My Code Anymore
items.text: AI-assisted programming raises distinct questions about who produces code, who feels ownership of it, and who is responsible when it fails. This research note examines these distinctions through a hypothetical enrollment failure and a selective reading of the literature. Identifying the producer of a defective expression does not, by itself, determine the duties of reviewers, release decision-makers, or service operators. Collective ownership likewise leaves those duties to be specified. The discussion then considers how quality engineering can evaluate both generated implementations and the processes that produce them. Acceptance criteria should be justified by the required service outcome, with component checks contributing evidence toward that outcome. This perspective also permits comparison with systems that perform a task without generating a separate program for it. Such substitution would change the object of authorship while leaving the service obligation intact. The note reports no new empirical results; it proposes distinctions and evaluation questions for AI-assisted software production.

items.text: Combining search with function approximation has driven major advances in game-playing programs, making self-play algorithms more competitive than ever. items.text: Large Language Models are increasingly deployed as information intermediaries, yet measuring their political behavior remains fragile because questionnaire results mix model dispositions with measurement artifacts and response-elicitation biases. We introduce a robust Political Compass Test evaluation framework that samples 300 configurations across an eight-dimensional perturbation space varying language, framing, instructions, answer format, option order, and persona wording. items.title: Latent-to-Latent Flow for Volumetric Stochastic Segmentation
items.text: Uncertainty arising from inter-observer variability in medical image segmentation plays an important role in developing treatment plans. Research in this area is inhibited by the lack of multiple annotations for large-scale medical datasets, especially for volumetric data, which suffers from additional scaling and computational complexity challenges. Flow matching has emerged as a powerful framework for generative modelling and has also been demonstrated to maintain strong performance when working with latent representations of images. In this work, we introduce a latent-to-latent flow technique for stochastic segmentation of medical volumes via encoded representations of both the image and label space. We evaluate our method on two challenging applications covering delineation uncertainty for radiotherapy planning and multiple organ structure segmentation, improving efficiency up to 14x compared with full resolution models while maintaining clinically relevant performance.

items.title: How AI Models Manage Epistemic Authority: A Taxonomy and Comparative Analysis of Responses to User Disagreement
items.text: Large language models are increasingly used as sources of advice and information, including in high-stakes settings, yet little is known about how they respond to user disagreement. We study how a model manages its epistemic authority, referring here to its claim to knowledge, competence, or the right to advise, once a user challenges its answer. Building on Conversation Analysis, we introduce a taxonomy of six challenge types and a four-layer framework for analysing each response: whether the original claim is maintained or changed, where authority is located, how the disagreement is socially managed, and what kind of evidential support is offered. We construct a new dataset of 2,310 controlled challenge scenarios and 32,340 corresponding responses from 14 models, and analyse them using our framework with an LLM-as-judge pipeline, providing a vocabulary which future evaluation and benchmark design can build on.
